claims.text: The damaged nickel-based superalloy has coarse columnar grains.
The damaged nickel-based superalloy contains localized microsegregation.
The damaged nickel-based superalloy is inherently susceptible to hot cracking.
FSP can be performed on this system at temperatures well below its melting point.
A tool rotation rate of 300–600 rpm is suitable for the proposed FSP treatment.
Real-time thermocouple feedback will maintain uniform FSP conditions.
The proposed FSP treatment will produce a uniform surface layer.
The proposed FSP treatment will refine the surface-layer grains through dynamic recrystallization.
The proposed FSP treatment will substantially reduce microsegregation and chemically homogenize the surface layer.
Severe plastic deformation during FSP initiates dynamic recrystallization.
Dynamic recrystallization breaks down coarse columnar grains.
FSP eliminates local chemical inhomogeneities during repair.
Uneven repair microstructures promote cracking.
The FSP-treated surface will have greater hardness than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The FSP-treated surface will have better fatigue resistance than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The FSP-treated surface will have better corrosion resistance than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The FSP-treated surface will have better wear resistance than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The FSP-treated surface will exhibit markedly less hot cracking than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs retain microsegregation and coarse grains that cause persistent hot cracking.
The intervention is effective only when the affected surface layer is thin enough to benefit from surface processing and service does not exceed the modified layer's thermal or mechanical limits.
